recent_posts.title: Dirty Frag: a zero-day universal Linux LPE
recent_posts.summary: Hyunwoo Kim has publicly disclosed Dirty Frag, a zero-day local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerability affecting all major Linux distributions. Similar to the recently disclosed Copy Fail flaw, it allows immediate root privilege escalation. The disclosure was forced early after an embargo break, meaning no patches or CVEs currently exist. Kim has released exploit code, a script to remove vulnerable modules, and a full write-up including the disclosure timeline.

recent_posts.title: An update on KDE's Union style engine
recent_posts.summary: The Union project, KDE's unified styling engine designed to support all KDE technologies for application theming, has reached a milestone where its Breeze implementation is nearly indistinguishable from the original. The team has tested it across multiple applications and plans to include Union in the upcoming Plasma 6.7 release (expected mid-June). It may be enabled by default, and users will have a way to try it out regardless.

recent_posts.title: Security updates for Thursday [LWN.net]
recent_posts.summary: A curated list of security updates released on May 6-7, 2026 across major Linux distributions including AlmaLinux, Debian, Fedora, Mageia, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Ubuntu. Packages patched include kernel, apache2, openssh, openssl, dovecot, curl, python3, systemd, wireshark, and many others across multiple distribution versions.

recent_posts.title: Three stable kernel updates
recent_posts.summary: The Linux stable kernels 7.0.4, 6.18.27, and 6.12.86 have been released, each containing a new set of fixes and updates for their respective stable branches.

recent_posts.title: Incus 7.0 LTS released
recent_posts.summary: Incus 7.0 LTS, the container and virtual-machine management system, has been released with support through June 2031. Key changes include a new low-level backup API, built-in basic S3 operations replacing the unmaintained MinIO project, and removal of cgroups v1 and xtables (iptables/ip6tables/ebtables) support. The first two years will include bug, security, and minor usability fixes via point releases, followed by security-only maintenance for the remaining three years. A total of 204 contributors participated between the 6.0 and 7.0 LTS releases.

recent_posts.title: The retirement of the PHP license
recent_posts.summary: The PHP project has officially retired the PHP License and relicensed its code under the three-clause BSD license. The process involved tracking down original PHP Group members for written consent, obtaining sign-off from Perforce Software (successor to Zend Technologies) on the Zend Engine side, legal review by an attorney, a six-month community discussion period, and a unanimous vote.

recent_posts.title: Alpine Linux systems currently offline
recent_posts.summary: All Alpine Linux systems hosted on Linode, including its GitLab instance, are currently suspended due to a billing issue. The team is working to resolve it, but services remain offline in the meantime.

recent_posts.title: NetHack 5.0.0 released
recent_posts.summary: NetHack 5.0.0 has been released, marking a major milestone for the classic dungeon-exploration roguelike game. The release brings C99 standard compliance and over 3,100 bug fixes and changes. Note that saved games from previous versions are incompatible with this new release.

recent_posts.title: Kernel prepatch 7.1-rc2
recent_posts.summary: The second Linux 7.1 kernel prepatch (rc2) is available for testing. Linus notes it is not small and suspects the continued pattern of more patches than usual is likely due to AI tooling, a trend also observed in the 7.0 release cycle.

recent_posts.title: NHS plans to close open source repositories over LLM security fears
recent_posts.summary: Terence Eden criticizes the UK's National Health Service (NHS) for planning to close nearly all of its open-source GitHub repositories, citing concerns about LLM tools like Anthropic's Mythos becoming better at finding security vulnerabilities. Eden argues the decision is misguided: most NHS repos contain datasets, internal tools, and front-end code with no realistic security risk. He points to the COVID Contact Tracing app, which was open-sourced and installed on millions of phones without causing any security incidents. He also notes the move contradicts the UK government's own Tech Code of Practice, which mandates being open and using open source.

top_posts.title: Git 2.54.0 released
top_posts.summary: Git 2.54.0 has been released by maintainer Junio Hamano. This release includes contributions from 137 people, 66 of whom are first-time contributors. Notable changes include the addition of Git history rewriting functionality and mobile-friendly improvements to gitweb, Git's web interface. Hamano announced he will be taking a couple of weeks offline following the release, with no designated interim maintainer but trusting the community to self-organize.

top_posts.title: Zig 0.16.0 released
top_posts.summary: Zig 0.16.0 has been released after 8 months of development, incorporating contributions from 244 contributors across 1183 commits. The headline feature is 'I/O as an Interface', alongside language changes, compiler improvements, build system enhancements, linker updates, fuzzer improvements, and toolchain updates.

top_posts.title: Firefox 150 fixes 271 vulnerabilities found by AI security model
top_posts.summary: Firefox 150 includes fixes for 271 vulnerabilities discovered by Claude Mythos Preview, an AI model that can reason through source code to find security bugs the way elite human researchers do. Mozilla argues this is ultimately good for defenders: AI-assisted discovery makes vulnerability finding cheap and widespread, eroding the attacker's traditional advantage of concentrating expensive human expertise on a single high-value bug.

top_posts.title: Analyzing what LLM-based Sashiko code reviews actually flag
top_posts.summary: Brian Exelbierd analyzes data from Sashiko, an LLM-based code review tool used in the Linux kernel's memory-management subsystem. He investigates two hypotheses: whether Sashiko flags pre-existing bugs in code not directly changed by a patch, and whether the same pre-existing bugs surface repeatedly across multiple reviews. Using Sashiko's public API, he finds that reviews are bi-modal — most don't include comments about unchanged code, but those that do tend to have several such comments, suggesting potential duplicate noise on mailing lists.
